lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- Who Judges a State?

lesson.grammar_point: defining and non-defining relative clauses with who, which, whose and where

listenings.text: Every year I give my students a case and ask them who should win, and every year they start in the wrong place. The first question in international law is not who is right. It is whether the court has jurisdiction. National courts have jurisdiction almost automatically: if you live in a country, its courts can judge you. International courts are different. A state is judged only if it has agreed to be judged, and that consent can be given in a treaty, in a special agreement, or in a declaration made years before the dispute began. So when a court says it has no jurisdiction, it is not saying the state was innocent. It is saying that the question was never allowed into the room. Remember that distinction, because it appears in almost every exam I write.

Listeners often ask us a fair question. If an international court orders a country to do something, and the country simply does not do it, what happens next? The honest answer is that there is no international police that arrives at the border. Enforcement works in quieter ways. A ruling that is ignored damages the reputation of the government that ignores it, and other states remember that in their next negotiation. Some courts send the case to a political body, which can put diplomatic pressure on the state. And inside the country, lawyers and judges often use the international ruling to change national law, one case at a time. Researchers who study these courts say that full compliance is rare, but partial compliance is common, and it often arrives years after the ruling.

paras: When a news report says that a case has gone to an international court, most readers imagine one building where all the world’s disputes are decided. In reality there are several courts, which answer very different questions, and students who confuse them usually make the same mistake: they ask who was right before asking who has jurisdiction.

The International Court of Justice, which sits in The Hague, is the principal court of the United Nations. It hears disputes between states, and only between states. No individual can file a complaint there. Its fifteen judges can rule on a case only when the states involved have consented to their jurisdiction, and member states of the United Nations have agreed to comply with its rulings. The court can also give advisory opinions, which are requested by United Nations bodies rather than by a party to a dispute.

The International Criminal Court, whose headquarters are also in The Hague, works the other way around. It judges individuals, not states, for crimes such as genocide and war crimes. It was created by the Rome Statute, which entered into force in 2002, and it acts only when national courts are unable or unwilling to do so.

For a Brazilian citizen whose rights have been violated by the state, the path is regional. A complaint is first filed with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and only the Commission or a state can take the case to the Inter-American Court, which is based in San José, Costa Rica. Brazil accepted that court’s jurisdiction in 1998. Its rulings are binding, but, like every international court, it depends on the state to put them into practice.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from the public descriptions of the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and the Inter-American human rights system.

tips: It is the power that a court has to hear and decide a particular case.

tips: The higher court upheld the first ruling, but a different court overturned another one.
